newsitem.title: UK: Copper backwardation to hot up as stocks dwindle.
newsitem.headline: Copper backwardation to hot up as stocks dwindle.

text.p: Backwardations in the copper market on the London Metal Exchange (LME) are expected to ratchet higher in coming weeks as published warehouse inventory figures show fresh falls, traders said on Thursday.

LME warehouse stocks, now at 109,175 tonnes, are forecast dropping on Friday by between 5,000 and 15,000 tonnes. A decline under of 10,000 tonnes will bring overall inventories under 100,000 tonnes for the first time since July 1990.
"The shorts are getting larger, the stocks are getting smaller, so something will have to give," one trader said.
The forward market is at an impasse at present as major players manoeuvre to keep prices within certain bands, partly to prevent options being declared but also to protect underlying positions.
Instead, copper's cash/threes backwardation is the obvious area where the pressure will show, and traders think an $82/87 premium now is likely to be above $100 soon.
"A lot of people have been willing to sell the market, even though stocks have been going down," said a trader.
The short positions that are building up in December and in January 1997 have reached levels that are far in excess of the current LME stockpile.
Even though the inventory trend is likely to be reversed by year-end, with stocks maybe back to around 120,000/130,000 tonnes, this will not be enough to satisfy the shorts.
"What has happened is that some of the shorts sold a few months ago as the backwardation started to widen. As these dates become prompt they have a problem," a senior trader said.

"They want to protect their position, so they won't buy back. Instead, they borrow, moving the position forward, and also sell the market to keep it within the range, so the overall position may be getting much bigger," he said.
And when the crunch comes, these speculative shorts may be in for a surprise, as the nature of the market has changed since the exit of Yasuo Hamanaka, others said.
"In the past there was always one person who had the warrants and was prepared to lend. So the shorts could always cover back - at a price," one said.

In June, Sumitomo Corp of Japan fired Hamanaka after it alleged that he admitted running up losses now put at $2.6 billion in 10 years of unauthorised trading. Hamanaka has since been arrested and charged with fraud.
"Because we don't have one single person controlling the market any more, this is more of a real market than it has been for a long time," a trader said.
